title: The curious economics of tipping
text: Tipping is a habit that economics cannot quite {{1}}. In most of the world it is a small, optional {{2}} for good service; in the United States it is a hidden wage, {{3}} by custom to around a fifth of the bill, without which restaurant staff could not pay rent. Historians trace the custom to imported European habits after the Civil War, {{4}} by employers who preferred tips to salaries — a practice so disliked that six states banned it, laws later {{5}} unconstitutional. The effects are measurable: tipped workers earn unevenly, face pressure from customers they must please, and the system {{6}} discrimination, since tipping correlates with a server's appearance as much as the service. Economists also note the {{7}}: tips barely respond to service quality — diners tip nearly the same whether the meal is flawless or disastrous. Yet reform {{8}}: no restaurant can unilaterally abolish tipping without losing staff to competitors who keep it. A custom everyone quietly dislikes, propped up by everyone's refusal to go first: no wonder economists find it fascinating.

gaps.explanation: 'economics cannot quite explain' — account for; expunge = erase completely, extol = praise highly.
'an optional bonus for good service' — an extra on top; bounty = a reward offered, often by authorities.
'pegged by custom to a fifth of the bill' — tied to it, as currencies are pegged to others; plug = block or publicise.
'championed by employers who preferred tips' — energetically promoted; chaperone = accompany and supervise.
'laws later declared unconstitutional' — formally ruled; defer = postpone out of respect.
'the system rewards discrimination' — gives it a payoff; regale = entertain with stories.
'economists note the oddity' — the curious fact; odyssey = a long eventful journey.
'yet reform stalls' — loses momentum; install = fit equipment, strew = scatter.
